newsitem.title: UK: Small rise in UK rates seen after May election.
newsitem.headline: Small rise in UK rates seen after May election.

text.p: Britain's Conservative government, trailing badly in the polls as election day looms, seems certain to keep interest rates unchanged at six percent despite pressure from the central bank, a Reuters survey showed on Friday.
But rates look set to rise after the May 1 election as political considerations wane and economic growth fuels inflation, according to the poll of 21 London-based economists.

The economists were unanimous in their prediction of no change in the base rates after next Thursday's monthly monetary meeting between Bank of England Governor Eddie George and Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke.

The economists said Clarke, who has the final say on setting central bank's minimum lending rate, would be committing political suicide if he were to increase the cost of borrowing so close to the election.
High levels of property ownership in Britain make the official rate offered by the Bank of England for borrowing or lending money of intense public interest and a potent political tool.
"A change is more likely to take place in July or August," said Andrew Schofield, senior economist at BSL Business Strategies.
George's advice at recent meetings with Clarke has been for a small upward rise to keep inflation at bay.
All of the economists, who were surveyed on Friday, said they expected George's position to prevail after the election, which the opposition Labour party is heavily tipped to win.

"The near-term inflation profile is favourable but by end-1997 we will see inflation trending up. The new government will have to make a pre-emptive move," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist at Bank of America, who predicted base rates of 6.75 percent by the end of the year.
"We have the same assumption no matter who gets in," said Natwest Group's Patrick Norwood, who predicts a rate of 6.5 percent by end-1997.
The economists' forecasts for end-1997 interest rates ranged between the current six percent and eight percent. The median forecast was 6.75 percent.

But economist Garry Young, of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, said that the perils of inflation were currently being overstated and although a Labour chancellor would be forced to raise rates, they would soon come down again.
"We see very little inflationary pressure just now, so there is no need for rates to go up," said Young.

"(Labour finance spokesman Gordon) Brown may need to gain some credibility with the markets and so he may go for a small rise in the middle of the year. But we see a subsequent fall at the end of the year, when the lack of inflationary pressure becomes apparent," he said.
